div2.head: BOOK III
div2.p: [III.1.1] When these events were reported to Nero, who was in the regions of Achaea, where he had gone to practise tragic songs so that he might carry off a theatrical crown from many rivals—one cannot tell which was more shameful: that an emperor appeared on stage, or that he filled the stage with his crimes, disgracing Orestes by his singing and re-enacting him by murdering his own kin—great fear seized him. He dreaded not those imitations offered by the games but the gravest dangers of war. Thus at last he recovered his senses from the obscenity of theatrical pleasures and the frenzy of his madness for the murder of kin. Turning to the concerns of the commonwealth, he growled and raged within himself that the Roman commonwealth had suffered so great a disaster through its commander’s negligence rather than its adversaries’ valour. He tried indeed to feign boldness, but fear gave him the lie. He also tried to put on an appearance of greatness of spirit, as though his mind stood above the distress of events, but he was racked with anxiety over whom to choose as commander to wipe away the disgrace and bring the war to an end.

[III.1.2] The final destruction awaiting Judaea pressed upon it, so that Nero put on a king’s role and pronounced a sound judgement in the voice of a far-sighted counsellor: Vespasian alone was the man to whom supreme military command in the regions of the East could rightly be entrusted. He was a man seasoned from youth in triumphant military service; he had settled in lasting peace the unquiet regions of Gaul, which had fallen back into war through German unrest and the ferocity of native rashness. Britain too, still hidden amid the waves, he had acquired by arms for the Roman dominion. Through the wealth of conquered Britain, Rome was thought richer, Claudius wiser in counsel and Nero braver. Thus they had celebrated trophies over subjugated nations whose wars they had not seen. Under this commander, I say again, Nero was terrible, Nero was to be feared, powerful abroad, safe at home, with Vespasian’s faithfulness and courage equally matched. How great was this man, whose arms concealed Nero’s vices among foreign nations, so that this mockery of human affairs and disgrace of emasculated impurity was even made illustrious by triumphs!

[III.1.3] Thus, when battle had to be fought at the farthest borders of the Roman world, Vespasian was chosen from all men; when war had been laid aside, Vespasian above all others was taken as a companion, so that no public enemy should remain and no domestic conspirator creep in. Worthy to anticipate kingship through his military service, he taught faithfulness and displayed valour. Nero sent him unwillingly, depriving himself of his protection, but the coming punishments for his crimes constrained him to leave himself unarmed, parted from so great a commander’s company. Galba would certainly never have undertaken his bid for imperial power had he not learnt that Vespasian was absent. But God arranged for a man to be sent to Syria who would both break the insolence of the Jews by the final destruction of their nation and the disgrace of captivity, and leave Nero without aid, although no man’s valour can impede heaven’s decrees. Yet the madman, on learning that a strong force of the Roman army had been crushed in the Jewish war, rose up against the Christians, so that the end he deserved drew near.

[III.2.1] At that time Peter and Paul, teachers of the Christians, were in Rome, distinguished in their works and renowned for their teaching. By the power of their works they had made Nero their enemy; he was captivated by the blandishments of Simon the magus, who had won his favour. Simon promised him, through deadly arts, aid in victory, the subjugation of nations, length of life and the safeguarding of his health; and Nero believed him, not knowing how to examine the nature of things. Indeed, Simon held the highest place in his friendship, since Nero even regarded him as the guardian of his health and keeper of his life. But when Peter exposed his empty pretensions and crimes, and showed that he counterfeited the appearances of things and accomplished nothing substantial or true, Simon became an object of mockery and was consumed by well-deserved grief. Although he had experienced Peter’s power in other parts of the world, he nevertheless reached Rome first and dared to boast that he could raise the dead. At that time a noble young man, a relative of Caesar, had died in Rome, to the grief of everyone. Many urged an attempt to see whether he could be raised. Peter was held to be most renowned for these works, but among the pagans no belief was accorded to deeds of this kind. Grief demanded a remedy; they went to Peter. There were some who thought Simon too should be summoned. Both came. Peter told Simon, who boasted of his own power, that he was giving him the first turn to raise the dead man if he could. If Simon did not raise him, Peter himself would not fail to do his part, so that Christ might bring aid to the dead man and enable him to rise. Simon, thinking that his arts would have the greatest power in a city of pagans, proposed a condition: if he himself raised the dead man, Peter should be killed for having insulted the Great Power—for that was what Simon was called—by challenging him; but if Peter prevailed, the same punishment should be inflicted on Simon. Peter agreed; Simon began. He approached the dead man’s bed and began to utter incantations and mutter baleful spells. The dead man appeared to move his head. A great shout rose from the pagans that he was already alive and was speaking with Simon. Anger and indignation turned against Peter for having dared to measure himself against so great a power. Then the holy apostle called for silence and said: “If the dead man is alive, let him speak; if he has been raised, let him rise, walk and talk.” The apparent movement of his head, he said, was a phantom, not reality. Then he said, “Let Simon be removed from the bed”; not even that apparent movement would then be seen. Simon was led away from the bed; the dead man remained without any appearance of movement. Peter stood farther away and, after briefly attending to prayer within himself, said in a loud voice: “Young man, rise: the Lord Jesus heals you.” And immediately the young man rose and spoke and walked and took food, and Peter gave him to his mother. When Peter was asked not to leave him, he said: “He will not be abandoned by the one who made him rise again, whose servants we are. Be at ease, mother, about your son; do not be afraid: he has his own guardian.” When the people rose against Simon to stone him, Peter said: “It is punishment enough for him to know that his arts have no power. Let him live and see Christ’s kingdom grow, even against his will.” The magus was tormented by the apostle’s glory. He collected himself and called forth all the power of his spells. He gathered the people and said that the Galilaeans had offended him and that he would leave the city he had been accustomed to protect. He fixed a day and promised a flight that would carry him to the seats on high, declaring that heaven lay open to him whenever he wished. On the appointed day he climbed the Capitoline hill and, casting himself from the rock, began to fly. The people marvelled, and many venerated him, saying that he was the power of God, not a man, since he flew about in his body, and that Christ had done nothing of the kind. Then Peter, standing in their midst, said: “Lord Jesus, show him that his arts are vain, lest these people, who are going to believe, be deceived by this appearance. Let him fall, Lord, but so that, while still alive, he may recognise that he had no power.” And immediately, at Peter’s words, the oarage of the wings he had put on became entangled, and he fell. He did not die, but went off to Aricia with a broken and crippled leg and died there. On learning this, Nero grieved that he had been deceived and left without support by the fall of so great a friend. Indignant at being deprived of a man useful and necessary to the commonwealth, he began to seek reasons for killing Peter. The time had now come for the holy apostles Peter and Paul to be called. Indeed, when the order had been given for their arrest, Peter was being asked to go elsewhere. He resisted, saying that he would by no means withdraw as though terrified by fear of death; that it was good to suffer for Christ, who had offered himself to death for all; and that this would not be death but immortality. How unworthy for him to flee the suffering of his own body! He had urged many through his teaching to offer themselves as sacrificial victims for Christ; according to the Lord’s word, it was his due also to give glory and honour to Christ in his own suffering. Peter wove together these arguments and others, but the people sought with tears that he should not leave them or abandon them as they were tossed amid the storms of the pagans. Overcome by their weeping, Peter yielded and promised to leave the city. The next night, after taking leave of the brethren and offering prayer, he began to depart alone. When he came to the gate, he saw Christ approaching him and, worshipping him, said: “Lord, where are you coming to?” Christ said to him: “I am coming to be crucified again.” Peter understood that this was said of his own suffering: Christ would be seen to suffer in him, as he suffers in each individual, certainly not through bodily pain but through a kind of merciful sharing in suffering or through the celebration of glory. He turned and went back into the city. Seized by the persecutors and sentenced to the cross, he asked to be fixed to it with his feet turned upwards, because he was unworthy to be fixed to the cross in the same way as the Son of God had suffered. This was granted, either because it was due, as Christ had foretold, or because the persecutor is not unwilling to grant an increase in punishment. Both he and Paul were killed, one by the cross, the other by the sword.

[III.3.1] But to return to our subject: Nero, disturbed by the grave news that affairs in Judaea had gone less than prosperously, placed Vespasian, a man experienced in war, in command of all the army in Syria. Vespasian acted swiftly, for there was no time for delay. He sent his son Titus to Alexandria to bring away part of the troops stationed there, while he himself crossed the Hellespontic strait and made for Syria on foot.

[III.3.2] Meanwhile the Jews, elated by their favourable circumstances, chose commanders for the war. They assigned the places over which each was to preside and the duties each was to perform. They placed Josephus, born of Gorion, and Ananus, the chief priest, in charge of the affairs of the city of Jerusalem, and especially of restoring its walls. Eleazar son of Simon burned to have some public office entrusted to him. Although he had brought under his own control all the spoils they had taken from the Roman army, especially rich and abundant spoils heaped up by Cestius’s greed and excessive plunder, they judged him more intent on establishing power for himself than on serving the common interest and decided to pass him over. But gradually, by courting individuals, giving and lavishing gifts, he contrived to have supreme control of all affairs entrusted to his judgement.

[III.3.3] Jesus, one of the priests, and Eleazar, a priest’s son, were also appointed commanders and entrusted with the defence of Idumaea, while reserving every prerogative in matters of the highest importance to Niger, the leader of all Idumaea. Jericho fell to Josephus son of Simon. Manasseh was entrusted with the region of Perea, situated beyond the Euphrates; it was given its name because those travelling to that region crossed the Euphrates. John Essaeus, another John, the son of Ananias, and the rest were assigned to various districts, which they were to defend with their care.

[III.3.4] Thus each kept to the duties entrusted to him, building walls and levying a force for war. Among them Josephus, going down into Galilee, diligently took care to fortify strongholds, restore defences and enlist the strongest men of the region and those readiest for war. He kept them from brigandage, maintained daily guard in camp, trained the soldiers after the manner of the Roman army, divided the ranks, distributed centurions and placed many in command, so that discipline could more easily be exacted from all and no one who abandoned his own duties could escape notice. He also trained them to recognise the trumpet’s calls to action and its calls to halt, keep their ranks, align their battle line and interlock their shields, so that these would serve as a wall against their assailants if a great force of the enemy fell upon them. He taught them to help those hard pressed, show compassion to the weary and take upon themselves the dangers of others. He not only taught the arts of war after the model of the Roman army, but also laid down before the war what would help them still more when fighting: a soldier should carry his own food and arms, fortify himself with rampart and ditch, forestall the enemy in pitching camp, obey commands and accustom himself to abstain from theft and plunder. He should reckon it his own gain if no loss were inflicted on the farmers. For what difference was there between the enemy and a man who himself carried off, in the enemy’s manner, what he found, except that it was worse to attack what was one’s own than what belonged to others, and to despoil allies rather than adversaries? A good conscience, he taught, was of the greatest value in war, because a man who knew himself to be implicated in no crime could rely all the more confidently on divine aid.

[III.3.5] Yet in these matters he found that envy among the wicked harmed him sooner than favour among the good benefited him. For although he had gathered about sixty thousand infantry, very few cavalry, about four thousand men who fought for pay, and six hundred chosen guards for his own body, he suffered so much from the Jews that he dreaded greater danger from his own people before the war than from the Romans in the war itself. I pass over the sedition stirred up because he was suspected of returning what had been stolen by brigands to those who had lost it, and especially to Agrippa and Berenice, to whom it ought rightly to be returned, lest they make the king more hostile. Yet to soften the people’s onslaught he said that the money, and all the things taken from Ptolemy, who had been carrying royal gold, clothes and other gifts, had been preserved for building the walls rather than compensating the owners. The Taricheans—for it was among them that this was happening—ought to consider whether they thought it should be reserved for restoring their walls or brought out for brigands to plunder. It certainly seemed shameful that he should suffer punishment because he had taken the better course.

[III.3.6] Thus, by winning their favour, he escaped both envy and danger. Again, when Tiberias sought King Agrippa’s favour and alliance, Josephus rushed out of the aforesaid city of the Taricheans and shut the gates, lest a messenger go to the city of Tiberias and reveal that Josephus lacked military support. He himself gathered from the lake as many fishing boats as he could find at the time and rowed towards Tiberias. But when he reached a place where the boats could clearly be seen by those in the city, although they could not discern whether they were empty of fighting men, he ordered them to disperse over the whole expanse of the lake. Their number would thus be thought greater, and no one would suppose them empty rather than full of warriors. Terrified at this, thinking themselves too weak to face so great a multitude, the people threw down their arms, opened the gates and poured out as suppliants to Josephus, who had approached as though leading a military column.

[III.3.7] They were asked what madness had put defection into their minds, and at whose instigation they were about to hand themselves over to the enemy. At the same time he ordered the helmsmen to take those who came out to meet him to Taricheae, and there he threw about six hundred councillors and many of the common people into chains.

[III.3.8] He also summoned Clitus as the ringleader of this crime and ordered him to pay the penalty by having his hands cut off. When Clitus begged that at least one hand be left to him, Josephus ordered him to cut off one himself, whichever he chose. Clitus then seized a sword in his right hand and cut off his left. Thus Tiberias was recovered. Sepphoris too, though it had attempted defection, was nevertheless kept among the allied cities of the Jews by Josephus’s vigour. For he preferred to defend what was his by more peaceful counsels rather than invade what belonged to others.

[III.4.1] But Niger the Peraean, Silas the Babylonian and John Essaeus gathered all the able-bodied young men in Judaea and made for Ascalon, a large city supported by strong walls, yet in need of resources and assistance. It was separated from the city of Jerusalem by seven hundred and twenty stades and by immense hatred. The Jews therefore, wishing to destroy a city hostile to them, gathered a force and rushed upon it. Antonius commanded the city with a smaller force of the Roman army than was thought capable of resisting the Jews.

[III.4.2] But he was a man of keener judgement and an equally prudent fighter. Leading out his cavalry, he allowed the Jews, scattered and relying more on their numbers than on their valour, to pass on towards the city. Then he charged them once they had advanced, exhausted them when they pursued, scattered them when they massed together, routed them when they fell into confusion, and chased the stragglers throughout the plain. Some, their position reversed, were pressed against the walls with their means of escape cut off; others headed in different directions, but were surrounded by the cavalry and cut down. Many fell upon one another and knocked one another down by their own onslaught. Thus, slaughtered until evening, they lost ten thousand of their men, with their commanders John and Silas killed as well. Only a few Romans were wounded in that battle.

[III.4.3] Yet the Jews’ rashness was not checked but blazed up. For grief kindled their boldness, and defeat provoked their desire for vengeance. They therefore took up arms with far greater fury, while the wounds of their injured men were still unhealed, and gathered more men than on the former occasion and rushed in. But Antonius caught them in prepared ambushes and, before they could come to grips, surrounded them with cavalry and ordered the encircled men to be struck down. Another eight thousand were killed; the rest were put to flight. Niger himself escaped and withdrew to a stronghold. It was a tower surrounded on every side by solid stone, which the Romans, unable to demolish it, encircled with fires. When it was set alight, he passed from the tower into a cave of some kind, hid from the enemy and escaped the fire. The Romans were secure in the belief that he too had been consumed in the blaze, but after the third day he was restored alive and vigorous to his own men, who were searching for his body for burial. Thus he was restored to the Jews, saved from the enemy, to their great joy.
[III.5.1] Meanwhile Vespasian, having crossed the Hellespont and passed through Bithynia and Cilicia, reached Syria and led the legions and other military forces he found there to Antioch.

[III.5.2] This city is undisputedly the first in Syria and is therefore regarded as its metropolis. It was founded by those who accompanied Alexander the Great in war, and named after its founder. The city’s site stretches to an immense length but is narrower across, since it is hemmed in on the left by a steep mountain face, so that the space for laying out the city could not be extended further. Necessity marked out the site: the high mountain would give the Parthians, breaking in by hidden and trackless routes, a hiding-place from which they could pour out upon unprepared Syria, arriving unexpectedly and attacking more readily, unless the city lay against the mountain like a barrier and blocked the exits to those approaching. Thus, if any of the barbarians climbed up, he would immediately be seen from the very heart of the city. Indeed, they say that when theatrical games were being celebrated in that city, a mime actor raised his eyes to the mountain, saw Persians approaching and immediately said: “Either I am seeing a dream or a great danger. Look, the Persians!” The mountain so overhangs the city that even the height of the theatre does not hinder the view of the mountain. A river cuts through its centre; rising in the east, it disappears into the sea not far from the city. The ancients called it Orient from the region of its origin, so that it is commonly thought to have given those places their name, though it received its name from them. With its streams made colder by their very rush, and with zephyrs constantly blowing through those parts, the whole city is cooled at almost every moment, so that it has hidden the East in the regions of the East. Within is fresh water; outside, nearby, are a grove interwoven with dense cypresses, and abundant springs. They call the grove Daphne because it never lays aside its greenness. The population is numerous and rather cheerful, as in most parts of the East, and wittier than almost all others, but more inclined to wantonness. The city was formerly ranked third among all the cities in the Roman world, but now fourth, since the city of the Byzantines has grown into Constantinople, once the capital of the Persians, now a bulwark against them. I think enough has been said about the city’s situation, for it does not seem necessary to linger over a description of its buildings. Since I have said that the east lies behind it, it is clear enough that the south lies on its left, Europe faces it in front, and the northern nations and Caspian kingdoms lie on its right; these were formerly most ready to invade Syria. But after Alexander the Great set the Caspian Gate upon the steep face of Mount Taurus and cut off every route for the peoples of the interior, he left the aforesaid city at peace, except perhaps when it feared Persian movements.

[III.5.3] In that city King Agrippa, with his whole force, was awaiting Vespasian’s arrival. Agrippa joined Vespasian’s company; Vespasian did not linger long. They began their journey together towards Ptolemais. The inhabitants of Sepphoris came to meet them at that city, asking Vespasian to confirm the peace long since concluded with Caesentius Gallus. Having praised their prudence in providing for their own safety by not provoking the Romans, and accepted their allegiance, he received them into friendship and strengthened their security with additional infantry and cavalry reinforcements, lest the instigators of the war, moved by the pain of being deserted, rise against them. For, with the Sepphoritans offering themselves to the Roman dominion, a kind of barrier guarding Judaea was being opened, so that the enemy had a clear route into Judaea. Sepphoris had stood in the enemy’s way, well placed to protect the whole nation. For besides its advantage of a more strongly fortified site, it was also the largest city of Galilee. This prompted us, since there are two Galilees, one upper and the other lower, connected and joined to each other, to distinguish the one from the other. But first we must speak of both.

[III.6.1] Syria and Phoenicia adjoin both Galilees. Ptolemais, with the bounds of its territory, and Mount Carmel mark off Galilee on the west. Carmel formerly belonged to the Galileans but is now attached to the territory of the Tyrians; adjoining it is the city of Gabaa, which once caused the Jews grievous destruction. On the east Ippene and Gadara mark it off with their own boundaries; these same limits were also laid down in ancient times for the region of Gaulanitis and the kingdom of Agrippa. On the southern side Scythopolis and Samaria meet it, each with its own territory, and do not allow it to extend beyond the streams of the Jordan. Tyre closes its northern reaches on the right-hand side, together with the whole region of the Tyrians, whose position sets the limits of Galilee’s extent. The two Galilees themselves are distinguished from one another as follows. The one called Lower Galilee extends in length from the city of Tiberias as far as the city named Zabulon, above the coastal parts of Ptolemais. Its breadth is undoubtedly drawn from the village of Xaloth, which is in the Great Plain, as far as Bersabe. From there Upper Galilee also begins, reaching as far as the boundaries of the village of Bachathe; that village also marks the limits of Tyrian land. The beginning of its length is the village of Thalla, and its end is Roth. Thalla adjoins the Jordan.

[III.6.2] From this one may understand how far Upper Galilee extends: its beginning is the Jordan, or the lands bordering it. Each Galilee, then, is distinguished by this measure of its extent. The land is rich, grassy, resplendent with diverse kinds of cultivation and dotted with trees, so that it attracts anyone by its charm and invites and rouses even one who shuns labour to the pursuits of cultivation. Indeed, not even a small portion of land there lies idle; it is thronged with many inhabitants. Cities are numerous, villages frequent, the multitude of people beyond number, so that a small village has fifteen thousand inhabitants in its district. Both Galilees are also surrounded by foreign nations on every side. Hence the people are warlike, trained from their earliest years in the trials of battle, abundant in numbers, ready in daring and prepared for all the arts of war.

[III.6.3] The region of Perea, however, surpasses them in size; we have said above where it got its name. Perea is larger, but Galilee is more productive: the whole of it is cultivated, and no part of it is barren of crops; all its land is rich and fruitful. Perea is more extensive but for the most part waste land that does not know how to be tamed by ploughing, and whose rougher furrows are not easily subdued. Yet part of it is soft for cultivation, fertile for use, pleasing to the eye, gentle to work, suited to grafted fruit trees and bearing all things. Trees set apart fringe its fields at the front, adorn them in the middle, and often protect the crops from excessive sun or cold. Above all, the land is clothed in olive trees, interwoven with vines or distinguished by palms. It is impossible to tell how beautiful it is when the rows of palms, struck by the wind, rustle together and the scents of the dates pour forth more sweetly than usual. Nor is it surprising that all the charm of greenery is there, where the fields are flooded and watered by the pleasing courses of rivers flowing down from the high ridge of the mountains, so that the land, teeming with snow-white springs, is possessed amid envy and desired with delight. Its length runs from Machaerus as far as Pella, that is, from south to north; its breadth, from Philadelphia as far as the river Jordan. That is to say, on the east it is bordered by the fields of Arabia, while on the west it is clearly seen to extend as far as the river Jordan.

[III.6.4] The region of Samaria also lies midway between Judaea and Galilee, beginning at the village named Eleas and ending in the land of the Acrabatteni. It is similar in nature to Judaea and differs from it in no respect. For each has mountains and plains, according to the diversity of its places: neither spreads entirely over plains, nor is it broken everywhere by mountain crags, but each has the charm of both kinds of terrain. The soil is loose and soft for cultivation, and therefore suited to grain, almost second to none in its fertility and certainly ahead of all others in the ripening of its crops. For when grain is still being sown elsewhere, it is harvested here. Nowhere is the appearance and very character of the grain held to be finer. The water is fresh, fair to look at and sweet to drink, so that, judging by the excellence of these elements, the Jews thought that this was the land promised to their fathers, flowing with honey and milk, although God had pledged them the privilege of resurrection. Divine mercy had indeed bestowed both, provided that they kept faith; but both were taken away from faithless souls, here by the yoke of captivity, there by the bond of sin. The region is wooded and therefore rich in livestock and abundant in milk. Indeed, nowhere do flocks bear udders so swollen with milk; its wild and grafted fruits surpass the abundance of every other region. Both Samaria and Judaea are filled with a multitude of people, so that it seems to me that the Jews took this as the basis for their interpretation of what is written, that none among them was barren or unfruitful, although the law had laid this down concerning the fruitfulness of merits and the fertility of virtues.

[III.6.5] Samaria begins at the boundaries of Arabia, at the village named Jordani, and ends to the north at the village of Borceus. The breadth of Judaea runs from the river Jordan as far as Joppa. For it begins at the springs of the Jordan and at Mount Lebanon and spreads as far as the lake of Tiberias. Its length also begins at the village of Arfa and extends as far as the village of Julias, where Jews and Tyrians live together. In the middle of Judaea the city of Jerusalem is called, as the wise have thought fitting, the navel of the whole region. The region abounds in inland resources and is not deprived of those of the sea, since it stretches as far as Ptolemais and fringes that whole sea with its shores. There are many cities, but Jerusalem stands out among them all, like the head in a body, which does not overshadow its limbs but governs them and serves as their protection and beauty. Thus, though with fitting brevity, we have not omitted what needed to be indicated about Judaea and the neighbouring regions.

[III.7.1] The military reinforcements granted to the Sepphoritans also raided the neighbouring regions, claiming unrestricted authority to plunder under the guise of the war being waged by the Jews against the Roman dominion. Josephus, eager to avenge the wrong done by such harsh treatment, therefore gathered a great number to his side and pressed on to storm the city of Sepphoris. He sought either to recall them to alliance with Judaea or, if they resisted, to overthrow them in utter destruction, if he could. But he failed in both attempts: he could neither dissuade them from their choice of union with Rome nor overthrow the city, which he himself had strengthened with such defences that it could not be taken even by the Romans, who were far superior. Thus the attempted assault, without achieving anything, sounded the trumpet and stirred up war throughout the region. They laid waste to everything day and night, burning buildings, plundering estates, killing all whom they captured who were fit for war and subjecting the weak to slavery. All Galilee was filled with fire, blood and plunder, spared no misery and disfigured in every aspect. Whatever had survived fire or slaughter was reserved for captivity. Compared with the evils of captivity, what had a little before been judged more bitter was preferable.

[III.8.1] These events were a kind of prelude to the war before Titus arrived. As soon as he had crossed from Achaea to Alexandria, he brought the soldiers according to his father’s command and came to the city of Ptolemais. There, with the fifth and tenth legions joined and the fifteenth also added—these were the most outstanding troops—and with the army of Romans and allies assembled, they began a savage and memorable war.

[III.8.2] For when, after initial successes under the command of Placidus, good fortune had turned to adversity, Vespasian set out with his son from the territory of Ptolemais in a more hostile spirit and plunged into Galilee. He learnt that they refused peace, although he had given them the chance to condemn their secession if they thought they should look to their own interests. He utterly destroyed Gadara, finding it empty of fighting men, since all the stronger men, distrusting its weak defences, had withdrawn to more fortified places. He therefore spared none of those he found, but ordered them all to be killed, with no regard for age and no pity for weakness. He carried this out less by the right of war than from grief at Cestius’s battle and hatred poured out upon the Jews. Indeed, he ordered not only the city but also the villages and towns to be burnt. Nor was his anger unjust, since after such insolence he had given them the opportunity to amend their error, and they had not obeyed.

[III.8.3] Josephus had passed from that city to Tiberias before the Roman army drew near, but his flight had inspired more fear than his presence had inspired confidence. For they were terrified by this very fact, that Josephus judged himself unequal to waging war against the Romans. His only hope was that the Jews might abandon their zeal for war: that was the course he preferred. If they chose war, he preferred to appear faithful to his fellow citizens by facing danger rather than a traitor by avoiding it. For his greatest concern was not to disgrace the military honour entrusted to him. He therefore wrote to the city of Jerusalem that war was upon them and that they should reply speedily. They must deliberate promptly whether they preferred peace or battle. He conveyed these matters briefly, inclining to neither side, lest he be judged either a fearful soldier or an obstinate rebel.

[III.9.1] He again went from the city of Tiberias to Jotapata, either because it was better fortified than the others and therefore very many of those readier for war had gathered there, or because Vespasian had sent many of his men there to make a road. The route through the mountains was difficult, rocky and rough for infantry, but impassable and insurmountable for cavalry. In four days, therefore, the stretches of road were opened up so that narrow passages would not hinder them, and a route was prepared by which the whole army could pass more easily. On the fifth day Josephus crossed over there and raised the downcast spirits of the Jews. When Vespasian too was informed that Josephus had gone there, he gained an incentive to hasten his march, since he thought it a shortcut to finishing the war if the commander and the people readiest for war were captured.

[III.9.2] He therefore arrived with the army and on the first day allowed time for the soldiers to be refreshed with food, so that the cares of war would not assail them when they were tired from the march. On the following day he enclosed the city with a double battle line and a third line of cavalry. When the Jews saw that they were hemmed in and besieged on every side, with no place of escape, they took courage from their very despair. For nothing makes a soldier readier for war than the necessity of fighting and the precipice of danger.

[III.9.3] Vespasian pressed them with javelins; he pressed them with arrows. Many of the Jews who had advanced beyond the walls were also wounded by skilfully aimed missiles, yet they remained unafraid. Roman valour tried every means, and wherever it perceived weaker defences in the walls, there it pressed with a greater force. Shame armed the Romans; hope armed the Jews, who longed to open with the sword a way to their last chance of safety. The Jews endured grievous onslaughts and returned attacks no less daring. Skill with valour fought on the Roman side, fury with rashness on the Jewish. They were therefore exhausted, the Jews fighting all day for safety and the Romans for triumph, when night broke off the battle.

[III.9.4] On the following day too, and on the third, and likewise on the fourth and fifth, they fought fiercely. But, as is usual in skirmishes, more wounds than deaths were inflicted, although the Jews often attempted sorties and the Romans assaults. Shame kindled the Romans to anger, because the conquerors of Hannibal and Antiochus and all nations were being delayed in battles with Jews. Such was their confidence in Roman valour that failure to win quickly counted as partial defeat. But their struggles were against nature more than against the enemy.

[III.9.5] For the city was hemmed in almost everywhere by precipitous crags. It was encircled not by a rampart and ditch like other cities, but by deep precipices which human eyes could not encompass and which no practical means could explore; the more closely one looked, the more deeply horror enveloped one. Only on the north, where the mountain fell away, did a single approach to the city lie open, though the ascent was steep. Josephus closed this with a wall and guarded it with defenders, so that an assault between the lower wall and the higher city would be dangerous for the besiegers, and whoever looked up could not judge what lay above. For the city itself, set on the brow of the mountain, is surrounded by a ring of neighbouring mountains as though by a natural rampart, hidden by a barrier native to the place, so that no one knows there is a city there before entering the city itself.

[III.10.1] Vespasian, unable to conquer nature, himself summoned it to his aid, so that by a prolonged siege he might force the besieged to surrender through lack of drink and food. But a supply of grain amassed long before kept the danger of famine at bay. The difficulty over water was very great, since there was no spring in the city, and the customary drought, with rain rare in those parts, had diminished their supply for drinking. All the water channels had been blocked to prevent water from reaching the city. Scarcity increased their thirst; nature resisted. Josephus proposed a device: to hang soaked clothes on the wall, so that, as water dripped from them little by little, it would be believed that they had water in abundance for washing clothes and no shortage of it for drinking.

[III.11.1] Discouraged by this, Vespasian was again fired with zeal to take the city. He gathered the whole army and shook the wall with engines; the ram battered it. Its appearance gave it this name: the head of a strong and knotty tree is clad in iron and covered with it like a ram’s forehead, which swells and juts out beneath an overlay of plates. From its centre projects something like a horn of more solid iron. The size of the tree is like that of a ship’s mast, which neither the storm of winds nor the swelling of sails would bend. Suspended by ropes tied to the upper, stout portions of timbers, it was driven against the wall by the strong hands of many men. Then it was drawn backwards and, held by its ropes like the beam of a balance, directed with greater force, so that the side of the wall, worn out by repeated blows, would give way and be hollowed out at the fractures, leaving an opening through which a path into the city’s interior would lie open to the Romans. At the first blow, therefore, the wall was shaken and trembled all over. At once everyone cried out, trembling as though the city had been taken, for fear that another blow would shatter the wall.

[III.11.2] But Josephus ordered sacks filled with straw to be lowered at the place against which the Romans were hurling the ram, so that the slack folds of the sacks would elude the blow and soften the whole impact of the ram. For solid things dashed against solid things do harm; against looser things their force is spent. Indeed, harder things give way more easily to softer things than softer things to harder. Rocks are dissolved by the washing of water, and a falling rock does no harm to water. When massive blocks are thrown into the sea, water retains its uses, but rock does not know how to retain its own amid the waves. Nor does falling marble break sand, while falling sand crushes marble to pieces. Yet the Romans too devised a way to counter the devices of the Jews, tying sickles to poles with which to cut the lowered sacks, so that, emptied of straw, they could no longer deprive the ram’s blow of its strength.

[III.11.3] When the thrust of the engine was thus renewed and the Jews saw themselves hard pressed, one of them, Eleazar, lifted a stone of immense size and dashed it from the wall onto the ram with such force that it shattered the head of the engine. Leaping also into the midst of the enemy, he seized the head of the engine and was carrying it to the wall, fearless in the sight of his adversaries and exposed to wounds. He was pierced by five javelins, but, paying no attention to his wounds, he bent his thoughts on how he himself might overwhelm the enemy with the falling stone. He therefore climbed the wall and stood conspicuous in his great daring, a victor over pain. He hurled himself and the stone onto the ram and fell with it, defeated indeed by death but victor over the engine. For in his own person he alone was lost to his country, but in shattering the engine he had saved the whole city from destruction. Netiras and Philip also threw themselves into the midst of the column, to turn back those whom they had attacked.
[III.11.4] Josephus, however, hurled fire to burn all the engines and soon burnt up a great many; but those burnt up were replaced.

[III.12.1] Vespasian pressed on and urged the attack so hard that an arrow struck him in the ankle. The Romans were alarmed when they saw their commander’s blood flowing. His son ran in agitation to his father, but Vespasian, whose strength of spirit rose above the force of the wound, forbade his son to be afraid and fired the soldiers all the more for battle, to avenge their commander’s injury. He himself acted as standard-bearer, rallying the army and driving it towards the walls; he himself urged the others into battle. Some pressed the enemy with arrows, others with missiles, others with ballistae.

[III.12.2] Such was the force of this engine, which hurled stones at the enemy, that one of Josephus’s companions standing nearby was struck and fell with his head shattered, and the back of his head was flung more than three stades away. A pregnant woman too, struck in the womb, had her infant hurled more than half a stade from the innermost recess of her generative organs.

[III.12.3] At last, when the Roman soldiers were already advancing victorious beneath the walls and strong forces on both sides were fighting at the very entrance, Josephus ordered scalding oil to be poured over the Romans, packed together as they were. It flowed easily from the tops of their heads to the soles of their feet. The heat of the glowing oil, no less than a burning flame, devoured every limb. Others nevertheless took their places, and in many cases streaming sweat even cooled the force of the oil. Although oil is of such a nature that it heats quickly and is slower to lose the heat it has absorbed, their zeal for victory made them conceal their hurt. They burned in spirit so that they felt no burning of the body. They reckoned the pain of that searing torment less than the loss of glory if those who had led the way in danger withdrew from battle as though they had no share in triumphs. They therefore strove to quench the burning oil even with their own blood.

[III.13.1] During this delay in the siege, the people of the neighbouring city of Japha had also grown insolent because the contest had lasted so long. Vespasian, provoked by this, sent Trajan, who held command of the fifteenth legion, with a thousand cavalry and two thousand infantry. He set out without hesitation, an energetic man skilled in the arts of war, and found an outcome suited to his zeal. For although the city was protected by the nature of the place and enclosed by a double wall, its people were not content to shelter within its fortifications but thought they should go out to meet the Romans. They dared to resist for only a short time, however, and in seeking to retreat inside the outer wall they also admitted the enemy, for the Romans entered along with them as they hurried in. When they fled to the inner wall, the gates were closed lest the Romans again burst in with them. Thus the Jews fought with God’s aid withdrawn from them, the aid by which they had formerly been accustomed to conquer. But they had offended by wicked crimes, and so the penalty they owed was exacted from them, that their sufferings might be bestowed upon the nations as a gift. Indeed, almost more of them were crushed in their wars with one another than by their enemies. The people of Japha are an example: they opened their gates to the Romans and closed them against themselves. For they themselves opened the first wall for the Romans to break in; the Jews closed the second wall to prevent the Jews from passing through. The enemy was therefore admitted, the ally excluded: the one admitted so that there would be no lack of a slayer, the other excluded so that the doomed man would not escape. Between the two walls the Jews were cut down at close quarters and struck from the wall at a distance. For many men of the Roman army, confined in the narrow space, climbed the wall and hurled missiles at those below. Thus the Galileans, more hostile to their own people than to their enemies, begged to be admitted through the entrance of the inner wall, but their own people resisted them. Fighting took place on the threshold of the gate, with Jews struggling against one another. Those on one side met an advancing formation with their swords, those on the other a resisting one. They died calling down savage curses on one another and declaring with their last words that they were suffering less than they deserved. Thus twelve thousand men were killed, all of them fighting men. Trajan, a man of the old discipline, thought that no one would now resist him or that the capture of the city would be easy. He reserved the crowning victory for Vespasian and sent to ask him to dispatch his son Titus to put an end to the battle. On his arrival they broke in and many people were slain, but victory did not fall to the Romans without toil and danger. When they entered the inner wall, all who were fit for war opposed them and, stationed in the narrow passages, made the outcome of the battle uncertain for the victors. Men and women fought from above, often hurling stones and every kind of missile they happened to find even at their own people. Indeed, at the very end they fought for six hours as though the battle were just beginning. At last, when those who had stood to resist were slain, the attack turned to the rest without order, without limit, without mercy. Old men were slaughtered with the young; women and little children were kept, not for pardon but for slavery. All the males were killed except those whom boyhood or infancy protected. Two thousand one hundred and thirty slaves were led away as booty, masters together with their slaves, now sharing the same condition: captivity had made them equals.

[III.14.1] Nor were the Samaritans exempt from misery. They had gathered and, according to their custom, climbed Mount Gerizim, which was sacred to them and where they were accustomed to worship. Hence the Samaritan woman also says in the Gospel, “Our fathers worshipped on this mountain,” and she was answered, “The hour will come when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.” For superstition had to cease and true religion succeed it, the shadow be done away with and the truth come, so that every person might worship God no longer on the mountain like the Samaritans, nor at Jerusalem three times a year like the Jews, but in spirit, in every place, lifting up pure hands and bending the knee in the name of Jesus. When, therefore, as we said above, they remained gathered on the mountain according to their rites, the very appearance of the gathering, or the disposition of those assembled, threatened war. They had not come to their senses even through their neighbours’ misfortunes, but were stirred all the more by envy at the Romans’ increasing success, and matters were close to an uprising. It was judged more prudent to forestall them, lest they break out into a greater calamity. Vespasian summoned the prefect of the fifth legion and sent him with three thousand men of both arms of the service. He judged it dangerous to climb the mountain at the outset, for the multitude of people and the precipitous terrain combined to inspire fear. He surrounded the foot of the mountain with his army and had a watch kept throughout the day to prevent anyone from coming down to draw water. Thirst tormented this great press of people, burning more and more fiercely in the heat, and many preferred to offer themselves to slavery or even death rather than perish from hunger or thirst. Cerealis—for that was the prefect’s name—judged from those who came down that all were exhausted. He encircled the mountain with his troops, promising safety if they laid down their weapons, and ordered those who refused to be struck down. Eleven thousand six hundred men were killed there.

[III.15.1] At Jotapata too, on the forty-eighth day, the Romans broke in at first light, while the inhabitants were still resting, exhausted by the great toil of the previous day. Titus was the first of all to enter, with Sabinus, and opened the way for the others. The higher ground was seized, and people still unaware of the entry were struck down everywhere in the narrow streets. Some paid the penalty in their beds, others newly awakened, others awake but weakened by hunger and drowsiness. Yet the whole city was still unaware of the force of the calamity. But when the army entered and roared with its battle cry, they rose with scarcely any thought but to meet death. Those who had tried to reach the higher ground were driven back and killed; the very crush had deprived those who might have had the strength to avenge themselves of vengeance. Those who prepared to resist were hidden from the battle as others rushed upon them. Others, exhausted by the long struggle, let their hands fall and offered themselves to be wounded, so that death at least might snatch them from such deadly spectacles of their own misfortunes.

[III.15.2] Misled by this unconcern of the dying, the centurion Antonius was asked by a man who had taken refuge in a cave to give him his right hand as a pledge of pardon and a guarantee of safety. He at once held it out, heedless of deceit and—alas, poor man!—too secure in his triumph. But the man struck him unawares with a dart and immediately ran him through, so that the Romans’ victory would not be complete.

[III.15.3] That day all who were found were killed. On the following days they were also brought out from underground chambers and other excavated caves, or killed where they were, except for little children and women. The slain counted over all the days numbered forty thousand; twelve hundred were led into captivity. The city and all its strongholds were overthrown and burnt with fire in the thirteenth year of Nero’s reign.

[III.15.4] Meanwhile Josephus was hiding in a pit among the city’s ashes, well aware that he was being sought with particular diligence as commander of the opposing force. He came out on the second day, but when he saw that every way was closed, he returned to the pit. On the third day a woman was found who knew Josephus’s hiding place and showed it to those searching for him. But forty men who had fled there were also hiding in the pit. They learned that Vespasian was inviting Josephus to hope for safety, first through Paulinus and Gallicanus, and afterwards through Nicanor. Nicanor was bound to Josephus by an old friendship, and for that reason had been sent to offer his right hand and was carrying out his appointed task all the more readily. They crowded round Josephus and assailed him with these words.

[III.16.1] “Now a greater ruin threatens the Jewish name, now fouler ashes threaten to bury and hide the discipline of a most illustrious lineage and overthrow all its honour, when Josephus is ordered to be kept captive for a triumph. What do these suddenly so earnest invitations from our enemies mean? What these unsolicited gifts of safety? They did not spare others when they begged for life: Josephus is summoned, Josephus is begged to live. Clearly they fear losing the pomp of a triumph, having no captive for Rome to gaze upon, no one for Vespasian to lead in chains before his chariot. Do you wish, then, to be kept for this mockery? And how will they triumph if the leader of those over whom they triumph is missing? Or what triumph is there if friendship is granted to the conquered? Do not believe them, Josephus. Life is promised to you, but things worse than death are being prepared. Roman arms may have conquered you; do not let deceit capture you. Their gifts are more terrible than their wounds: the former threaten captivity, the latter preserve freedom. Are you yielding, Josephus, broken by some softness of spirit, and do you wish to outlive your country? Where is the teaching of Moses, who asked to be blotted out of the heavenly book so that he would not outlive the Lord’s people? Where is Aaron, who stood between the living and the dead so that death would not devour the living people with its savage contagion? Where is the spirit of King Saul and Jonathan, devoted to their country, and that death for their fellow citizens, bravely undertaken, gloriously sought? The son called his father by his example; the father did not forsake his son in his resolve to die. Though he could have lived, he preferred to be killed rather than led in triumph by the enemy. He urged his armour-bearer, saying, ‘Strike me, lest these uncircumcised men come and strike me and mock me.’ Because his armour-bearer was afraid, he ran himself through with his own sword. He was worthy to be avenged by David in the prophetic spirit, because a man of Amalekite descent had falsely boasted of his death and thought to diminish the glory of the man who had snatched himself from the enemy by lying that he had killed him. He was worthy also to be praised by so great a prophet, who said, ‘Saul and Jonathan, lovely and most dear, inseparable in their life, and in death they were not separated, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.’ David himself too, when he saw the people struck by the angel, wished to turn the heavenly vengeance upon himself, so that he would not be spared while the people perished. Finally, where is the divine law, whose interpreter you have always been, which has promised the righteous everlasting immortality in exchange for this brief life? Where is the God of the Hebrews, who teaches the righteous to despise death, that they ought even to shun their earthly dwelling and fly back to the heights, to that region of paradise where God has consecrated devout souls? Do you now at last desire to live, Josephus, when you ought not—indeed, when it is not lawful, indeed, what is more, not fitting? Do you long to enjoy this light—I would dare to call it the light of slavery—which is in another’s power? So that the Roman may snatch it away when he wishes, or veil it in the darkness of prison when he wishes? So that you may long to flee from here and not be allowed to die? And with what sense of shame will you go to those whom you persuaded to die for their country? What excuse will you have for lingering so long? They are waiting to see what you do; surely they are already saying, ‘Why does Josephus delay, when he ought to have gone before us? Why does he follow so late? Why does he refuse to imitate his pupils, whom he urged to die for freedom?’ Are we indeed to endure your choosing slavery, champion of freedom, your binding yourself to the Romans as a slave, your preferring captivity to freedom? But suppose you wish to live: how will you obtain this from those against whom you have fought so often? How will they look at you, with what eyes, with what feelings? How will you wish to live under angry masters, even if you are allowed? Or who will not believe you to have been a traitor to your country when he sees you paid the reward of treachery? Choose which you prefer. One of these two things must be: your life will be either the reward of treachery or the punishment of slavery.” With these words they levelled their swords, adding, “If you consent to die, we offer our service as friends; if you refuse, we exact vengeance as men betrayed.”

[III.17.1] To this Josephus replied: “And who would wish to survive so much death? Who would choose to become an heir to sorrow? Who would not wish his soul to be released from this body of death, if it were permitted? But none may loose the bond except the one who bound it. The soul is joined to the body by the bond of nature. Who is the author of nature but almighty God? Who would dare to interrupt and dissolve this union of our soul and body, which is pleasing to God? If someone removes from his hands bonds imposed at his master’s command, without his master’s permission, will he not be condemned for having grievously wronged his master? We are God’s possession; we owe God service. As slaves let us await his commands, as prisoners let us preserve our bonds, as the faithful let us guard the good deposit. Let us not reject the gift of this life which he has given us; let us not shun the heavenly gift. If you reject a human gift, you are insulting: how much more ought we to preserve what we have received from our God? From him, then, we have received our being; it ought also to be for him to decide how long we exist. For both are marks of ingratitude: to depart sooner than he wishes and to live longer than the one who gave us life has willed. Did Abraham hasten before his time? Did Moses climb Abarim before he was told, ‘Climb Mount Abarim’? But he was told to climb, and he climbed and died. Like a good servant he awaited his master’s command. Job himself, who said, ‘Let that day perish on which I was born,’ nevertheless, beset by wounds and pains, did not break the bonds of this life, but asked to be released, saying, ‘Why is light given in bitterness, and life in the pains of the soul?’ He certainly praised death when he said, ‘Death is rest for a man,’ yet he did not seize it before his time but asked for it, as it is written: ‘I am shaken in every limb, and since I am impious, why have I not died? Why did I not fall from my mother’s womb into the grave? Or is not the time of my life short? Leave me to rest a little.’ Another holy man also says, ‘Bring my soul out of custody.’ He asks to escape, asks to be released from this body as from a prison. Yet none of the saints takes it upon himself, none seizes it before his time. If dying is gain, it is theft to seize it before the expected time; if living is good, it is sacrilege to reject it before it is demanded back. But you think it glorious to die in war. Nor do I deny that it is good to die in war for one’s country, good to die for one’s fellow citizens. But by the law of war I offer my throat if the enemy seeks it, if the Romans plunge in the sword—the Romans to whom God has granted victory over us, to whom he has consigned us because of our sins. Nor do I flatter myself because they promise to spare me. Would that they deceive me! I shall at least carry away this gain, that they feared me so much as to deceive me; I shall at least take this vengeance, that they break faith. I would rather perish by their brigandage than by my own. It is my brigandage if I lay hands on myself; if the enemy does so, it is a benefit. Thus, though they could grant this benefit by killing me, they thought to grant it in this way: they turned into brigandage what lay within their power: to kill a captive. But you promise me the service of your hands. Truly, we lacked a slayer, so that we should perish by our own crime! I do not wish to perish by my crime, nor by yours, which is more than mine, nor by our mutual crime. For this is what it means for each of us to lay hands on himself: to pay the price of reciprocal killing, so that each incurs guilt not only for his own blood but also for another’s. But the example of King Saul is brought forward: surely the man who was demanded as king against the divine will and earned God’s displeasure, whence he received a successor even while he was alive. A splendid example of a man who lacked God’s favour! Yet he wished to die because he could no longer live. He too, however, wished his companion to kill him; but the man thought it a crime and refused the service. So he turned his sword against himself not by following counsel but because he was denied that service. If he acted from fear of being mocked, why do you praise what belongs to fear? If he was not afraid, why did he first choose something else? I fear the Romans neither when they mock nor when they lie. Saul alone killed himself, not Jonathan, nor anyone else in our Scriptures. What wonder that he could kill himself, when he could even kill his son? Aaron stood between the living and the dead, and that belongs to valour, not rashness. For he did not inflict death on himself but did not fear death, repelling it with his body and standing in its way as it crept upon everyone. I am not Aaron, but neither am I unworthy of him: see, I offer my hands; let them strike as they will. If I can fear their hands, I deserve to perish by my own. If they spare an adversary, why should I not spare myself? If you ask why they wish to spare me, they admire valour even in an enemy. For such is the favour valour wins that it often pleases even an enemy. You yourselves also know how much destruction I have inflicted on the Romans, how by the long siege of the obscure city of Jotapata I diverted the conquerors of all nations from destroying the city of Jerusalem. At a small cost I played out the hazard of the whole war. Others have learned through my danger to desire peace. Perhaps we are spared for this purpose, that the others may not be deterred but encouraged. But you maintain that it is sweet to die for freedom. Who denies that either? Yet it is sweet to live with freedom. For the man who offers friendship promises freedom. But if he imposes slavery, then there will surely be a more fitting time to wish to die, if death is necessary. Now, however, they offer life; they do not wish to kill us. Both the man who refuses to die when he ought and the man who wishes to die when he ought not are timid. For who does not know that to wish to die in order not to die belongs to womanish licence and womanly fear? Indeed, frightened women, when they learn that some danger threatens them, are accustomed to throw themselves over a precipice. For in their narrow spirits they cannot sustain the weight of terror and the fear of death. But the steadfast man, who does not fear the present and thinks of the future, knows no trembling where there is no cause for fear. Indeed, it is written that ‘the souls of the effeminate will hunger’: they hunger because they do not have the food of valour, and so they hasten to death before their time. For one filled with the food of spiritual grace does not lay hands on himself, since it is written that ‘the mouth of the foolish calls upon death’. Again Scripture says, ‘And he who takes no care of himself in his works is the brother of him who destroys himself.’ Thus the man who strikes himself is condemned. For what is so contrary to the law of nature? What so contrary even to the nature of all living creatures? Love of themselves is implanted in all, even wild and untamed beasts. For the law of nature is strong: to wish to live and not to bring death upon oneself. Indeed, all kinds of living creatures cannot arm themselves with iron against themselves even if they wish. Humans may have invented the hideous noose of death; beasts know nothing of it. But the bites of beasts are their weapons, their teeth their swords. Yet when has anyone heard of a beast biting off one of its own limbs? Against others they use their jaws as weapons, upon themselves for kisses. For us too, what is so sweet as life, what so hostile as death? The man who protects life is a patron; the man who tries to seek our death is a plotter. Do we then wish to inflict on ourselves what we abhor in others if they attack us? And do we impose upon ourselves as a favour what we exact from others as a punishment? We prosecute a helmsman if he dashes the ship entrusted to him against a rock; do we ourselves destroy with iron the helm of our body entrusted to us and consign it to voluntary shipwreck? But you confront me with an early death once I have been brought into the enemy’s power. What shall I gain, then, if I inflict upon myself what I fear from the enemy, when it may happen that the enemy will not do what you urge me to do? It is just as if a helmsman, seeing a storm to come, sank his ship in the waves to avoid the storm. Or do you think we must forestall the adversary because he will exact more grievous torments? Or because you think it brave to use iron against ourselves? But seeking to gain by avoiding torments is a refuge of weakness, not a trophy of valour. Do we therefore cling to something that bears neither the marks of courage nor any practical gain? Why should I add that the sanctity of a deposit is violated? Almighty God gave us a most excellent treasure, enclosed it in this earthen vessel and entrusted it, sealed, to our keeping until he should please to demand it back. Is it not a crime in either case, to cast away the deposit when the giver has not demanded it back, or to deny it when he does? If violating a human deposit is disgraceful, how much more so is violating God’s deposit? The soul in this body is God’s deposit, a soul that cannot be subject to this death. For it is not constrained or bound by any bond of death, but seems to bring about death when it is released from the body and separated from the union entrusted to it. Why then do we inflict death before the deposit is demanded back, dismiss the soul as though it were of no use to us, exclude it from our house, and dissolve into earth the body deprived of its own beauty and grace? Why do we not await the command to depart from here? A soldier awaits the watchword, a slave the command. If either leaves without an order, the one is a deserter, the other a fugitive. The man who flees a human master is liable to punishment, even if the master he fled was wicked. Can we flee the best of all masters without being bound by the disgrace of impiety? Does it also escape our notice that God has stationed an angel around those who fear him? There is therefore someone to forbid departure unless a command has been received. If there is no command, there are no provisions for the journey. And how do we arrive without provisions for the journey? Who will receive us in that pure and secluded place? Who will admit us to those fellowships of holy souls? Adam hid because he had transgressed God’s command; he was shut out of paradise because he had not kept the order. He is asked, ‘Adam, where are you?’ as though he had fled, as though he were not present before God. Will I not also be asked, ‘Where are you, who have come without a command, whom I have not released from the bonds of nature? Take him into the outer darkness: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ We have learned that these acts are forbidden not only by human custom but also by laws. For some order those who have plunged iron into themselves to be cast out unburied. It is fitting that those who have not awaited their Father’s command should be deprived of burial in the earth, as though of a mother’s lap. Others cut off the right hand of the dead, so that the hand which fought against its own body in mad fury is separated from that body’s limbs. But this is the end suffered by the sacrilegious, or traitors, or killers of their parents. Those who have not acknowledged their true Father do not recognise themselves either. Thus they are either forbidden burial altogether or are not buried whole. Nor does paradise receive their souls, but the darkness of the underworld and savage torments. As I consider these things, although everything has been taken away, these alone terrify and frighten me: that I might inflict on myself what not even the enemy can inflict, and rob myself of those things of paradise which the Roman has not yet been able to take away—he can certainly hasten them, he cannot remove them—which alone I impatiently desire. For no desire for this life holds me, in which I have found nothing to delight me either among my fellow citizens or among my enemies. The former denied me peace, the latter robbed me of my country. Amid so many evils, what sweetness can remain in this life? Only you, almighty Father, author and arbiter of nature, grant me an honourable end. Break this bond of nature, restore my soul to its secluded places. Though the people be destroyed, their right taken away, their freedom broken, I shall not transgress your law by dying unbidden. I await your command; I await the release I desire from you. You have many to carry out your will: from you I await the command, from its executor the service. It is good to die, but if I die as a Hebrew, not as a brigand, not as an executioner, not as an enemy. Though I be defeated in war, I shall remain what I was born, so that I do not abandon the inheritance of Abraham our father. I shall not cross over into the number of the enemy to become my own slayer. I can offer myself to the enemy to be struck without loss of devotion; I cannot turn my hands against myself as an enemy without crime. Or is the fear that we may not be allowed to live according to the law? Truly, great is the freedom we now enjoy, when we are not allowed to die according to the law.”

[III.18.1] Josephus put forward these arguments to undermine the defence of voluntary death. But those who had once devoted themselves to death, unable to resist his words, surrounded him with swords as though ready to strike him at once unless he thought fit to consent. Surrounded, he called one man back with a commander’s authority and addressed another with a stern gaze and the consciousness of his own valour. He restrained one man’s right hand, bent another’s anger, soothed them with wholesome counsel. In different ways he wrested unreasoning fury from each man. For although the final turn of fortune had stripped the defeated man of his dignity, it had not wholly abolished their reverence for him. Little by little, therefore, hands were lowered and swords put away, but their resolve persisted.

[III.18.2] When he saw that he alone was held besieged by many, whether by some chance or by design he devised a way to reduce the number of those opposing him. “Let us entrust the order of dying to the lot,” he said, “so that no one may withdraw, since the lot embraces all. Let the condition of this lot be that whoever is drawn is killed by the man who follows.” Thus it would be the lot, not each man’s own will, that condemned him to death. “Let each therefore stand with the lot as judge, free from crime and free from captivity, so that he neither hastens the death to come at another’s will nor evades it at his own. No one will be able to refuse an outcome which either chance has brought about or God’s will has marked out.” The offer inspired confidence, and all agreed to the lot. Each man designated by lot offered himself to the next, ready to be killed. So it happened that when the rest had been killed, Josephus and one other survived the slaughter. It necessarily remained that either he would be condemned by lot, or, if he survived the destruction, he would be stained with his companion’s blood.

[III.18.3] He persuaded his companion that they should renounce the lot. Thus he escaped the battle within and was conducted by Nicanor to Vespasian. A crowd gathered to see him arrive, with almost all the Romans flocking together. Some wished to see cast down the man whom a little earlier they had seen in the highest honour, in command of the whole enterprise; others strove to mock the captive; others marvelled at the changes in human affairs, so varied and shifting. Many, with greater wisdom, groaned, reflecting in another’s fall that the same could happen to themselves. Titus was moved more than the rest by his innate gentleness of spirit: this man, lately a proud warrior, suddenly subjected to the enemy’s power, awaited his fate at another’s nod, shipwrecked in life, an exile from hope, uncertain of safety. So much could a moment in battle accomplish, that a brief turn of fortune made men unlike themselves, when either the powerful were cast down or the afflicted raised up. Thus the better part of them, namely those who held honour, offered gentler counsels. Yet Titus played the greatest part in securing Josephus’s safety with his father. Vespasian ordered him to be kept under guard, lest he slip away.

[III.19.1] A few days later Vespasian returned from there to Ptolemais and then hastened to Caesarea, the largest city of Judaea, but inhabited more by gentiles. They therefore welcomed the Roman army with applause and joy, not only because they desired the favour of Roman alliance, but also from an ingrained hatred of the Jewish people. With the loudest cries they shouted that Josephus, its leader, ought to be punished. Vespasian let this anger subside in silence, as the unreasoning anger of the crowd. Since both the season and the city were suitable for winter quarters, he stationed two legions in Caesarea, and the tenth and fifth legions in the city of Scythopolis, lest Caesarea be worn down by the burden of the whole army. The aforesaid city was therefore consecrated to Scythian Diana as a foundation of the Scythians, and was called the city of the Scythians, as Massilia was of the Greeks. The situation of the place shows that its founders, in their innate hardiness, chose open plains rather than ground suited to habitation. For open places bring more hardship than pleasure both in the harshness of winter and in the burning season of summer: in winter they lie more exposed to the cold, and summer’s heat is fiercer in places which receive the full sun without the delight of any green field. Thus the flat and coastal region of the aforesaid city was heated still further by the heat of the sea.

[III.20.1] Yet Vespasian was not free from the business of war. He learnt that very many people had gathered from different places at the city of Joppa and had restored it as a convenient base for piratical raids, repairing the buildings which Cestius had destroyed. Since the countryside had been devastated, they sought their means of subsistence at sea. He carefully investigated everything. They fitted out vessels suitable for brigands’ use and watched the passage of travellers, plundering almost all the trade of Phoenicia and Egypt. Their frequent raids spread such terror that they closed that entire sea, and fear of certain danger interrupted navigation. On learning this, he ordered a force of infantry and many cavalry to set out and enter Joppa by night. This was easily done, since no guard protected the city: it was thought that the Roman commander would give no attention to a city reported to be destroyed. The inhabitants were there, but did not dare resist the arriving Romans or deny them entry. They boarded their vessels, went beyond arrow-shot and spent the night at sea.

[III.20.2] The subject seems to require a brief account of the shore along Joppa, so that it may be clearly shown how the aforesaid city suffered a second disaster without any battle. The city has no natural harbour. Its seashore is rough and straight, but bends slightly into promontories at either end. There are deep-rooted cliffs and immense rocks projecting from the sea; although they rise from the sea’s depths, they also jut out into it. Hence the shapes of the places and the very appearance of the landscape seem to reveal that Andromeda was there when she was exposed to the sea monster, lending no small credibility to the ancient tales. When the opposing blasts of Boreas strike the shore, the waves rise to an immense height. Dashed against the rocks, they raise a mighty crash and, falling back into the waters, make that inlet so restless that there is more danger in harbour than in the open sea. While the boats which, as we said above, had put out from Joppa were tossing there, a violent wind, which those sailing in that region call Melamborium, swept down towards morning. At once, with the waves driving them, it threw the boats against one another and engulfed them. Some, their anchor cables broken, it drove against the rock. Others were heaved violently upwards against the oncoming sea as the sailors sought to escape the danger of the rocky shore or slaughter by the Romans, who had spread along it. A wave met them, towering above them in a lofty mass, overwhelmed them and sank them. There was nowhere to flee and no hope of remaining, since the wind drove them from the sea and the Romans shut them out of the city. The sound of the vessels colliding was grievous; the groaning of the men as they were crushed was unbearable. When they saw the sea breaking into their unsteady hulls, some, skilled in swimming, threw themselves overboard. Others, leaping towards boats drawing near, fell into the sea and were crushed by the collision of hulls. Many sank into the depths with their light vessels, having lost confidence in swimming clear. Yet death came with less torment to those who lacked the skill or any hope in trying. Those who attempted to swim were struck repeatedly by broken fragments of the ships, which crashed into their sides and hideously battered their wretched limbs. Or death overtook them as they were driven against the rocks, amid their very prayers to embrace the shore; yet they had what consolation they could in dying on land. The sight was therefore pitiable: the rocks were spattered with the brains dashed out of the unfortunate men, the shores wet with blood. You could have seen the sea stained with gore, everything filled with corpses. If any had escaped, they were killed as they approached the shore. For the Romans judged that the storm raged there not from the roughness of the place and the customary winds, but that divine indignation had stirred the sea, with the winds conspiring beyond their usual manner to prevent the Jews from escaping. They therefore feared to spare those whom God had not spared. Some killed themselves with the sword, thinking it more bearable to perish by the sword than by shipwreck. Others, trying to push boats away with poles, pierced them. Some drove back with oars or struck with a weapon those who had fallen into the sea, if they begged to be taken aboard by those in the boats. I have not passed over this, so that it may be clear that the Jewish people faced greater danger from themselves than from the enemy: they killed one another, as though all the things hostile to them together—sky, enemy, sea and rocks—were too little for their destruction. Four thousand five hundred dead bodies, which the sea had spat out, were therefore counted; the city was captured without battle and razed to its foundations.
