[III.20.3] Thus, within a short time, Roman hands destroyed Joppa for the second time. Vespasian thought this order just, lest pirate dwellings be established there again. Hence, although he was leaving, he left cavalry there with a smaller number of infantry. The infantry were to remain in the place, to prevent a band of brigands accustomed to brigandage from making any attempt; the cavalry were to range through the neighbouring countryside, villages and small towns, so that everything might be utterly destroyed and the inhabitants prevented from combining in any enterprise.

[III.21.1] While these events took place at Joppa, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, distant though they were, were not even so free from sharing the disaster. They heard what the Romans had done in Judaea, and especially that Josephus had been killed. They did not believe it, first because no informant had come to them from those places, and secondly because they thought that so great a commander could not readily have fallen into the enemy’s hands. Indeed, no messenger had survived so great a disaster. This very fact, that no informant survived, confirmed the report of utter destruction: everything had perished, nothing remained even to tell what had happened. An impression spread that exceeded any report. As the very silence terrified them in their uncertainty, everything they feared was believed. Far from anything going unreported, even things that had not happened were added. For rumour had also insisted that Josephus had been killed, and this brought the greatest grief to everyone.

[III.21.2] But when they learnt that he was living among the Romans, they pursued him with such hatred that they detested the life of the very man whose death they had first lamented, as a sign of either cowardice or treachery. Hence their agitation against the Romans grew greater, to avenge themselves on Josephus; and the more their fortunes declined, the more they were inflamed for war. Where there ought to have been an end, they took up a new beginning of evils. For the wise find in adverse outcomes a lesson in greater caution, so that the same things which have already gone badly may not happen again; but for the foolish they are an incentive to misery. Their allies’ danger ought therefore to have brought the people of Jerusalem to their senses, but because they refused to understand so that they might act well, it turned to their destruction.

[III.22.1] Vespasian, however, yielded to Agrippa’s request to spend about twenty days in Caesarea Philippi, a city of his kingdom, so that the very delay might allow the Jews to take better counsel for themselves and the army to rest a little from its toil. At the same time the troubled parts of Agrippa’s territory might recover their senses from the frenzy of agitation and discord. Their inhabitants ought to understand that, if they changed their course, they could be received through the king’s intervention, when such diligent exchanges of services bound the king and the Romans together. Indeed, Tiberias, near Caesarea, did not reject the remedy and found health. For it too seethed with a grievous disease: its people were divided against one another. Vespasian therefore decided to summon three stronger legions and send them to Scythopolis, dispatching his son on the business. This was the greatest of the ten cities, near Tiberias. From there he ordered Valerian to approach the walls with fifty cavalry, to urge peace and call those shut within to faithful alliance. The terror of the assembled army was to strike the unwilling, while the messenger of peace invited the willing. Valerian dismounted near the walls, and those who had approached more closely with him did the same. Jesus, the leader of a band of brigands, and his companions, who dared to advance with him, thought them contemptible for their small number. In a sudden sortie they drove them from their position and seized the horses which Valerian had brought, as his men withdrew together. Fools, they did not see that Valerian showed better judgement in yielding to their insolence than they did in taking spoils from those who offered peace.

[III.22.2] The elders, offended by the enormity of the deed, therefore left the city and came to beg Vespasian not to attribute the insolence of a few to the whole people. Vespasian immediately sent Trajan to the city to discover whether the people rejected the attackers’ rashness. By reporting that the people’s wishes agreed with the elders’ entreaties, he added credibility to the embassy. Thus pardon was granted to those who asked for it, especially since Vespasian saw the king’s concern for the condition of the whole city. On the king’s pledge that they would dare nothing of the kind thereafter, he willingly granted pardon for the offence.

[III.23.1] From there he made for Taricheae with an alert and well-equipped army, since a very great multitude had gathered at that city because of the strength of its position. Josephus had enclosed it with a wall, except where, inaccessible on foot, it was washed by the waves of Lake Gennesar. They therefore gathered vessels and clamoured for war on two fronts: if the battle on land turned against them, they would flee to their ships; if they gave way in a naval contest, they would return to the city and defend themselves with its surrounding walls. The defences of Tiberias and Taricheae were similar, but the characters at Taricheae were more desperate. The wall of Tiberias was stronger, but the fury of the Taricheans readier, so that, if necessary, they would throw everything together, naval contests with those on land, those on land with naval. At last, surrounded by the opposing army, they dared more than their strength allowed. Their rashness made no headway against the order of the Roman deployment and the valour of the veteran army. Before they suffered any destruction, they turned in flight and rushed to their vessels. They packed these together and fought as though in a close battle line, as if the contest were being fought hand to hand on land. An innumerable multitude was also awaiting the enemy on the plain. On learning this, Vespasian sent his son with chosen cavalry.

[III.23.2] When he saw himself surrounded by immense forces, he reported to his father that the enemy’s multitude was greater than had been supposed. But he called together those whom he had led out with him and fired them for battle with this address.

[III.24.1] “Men of Rome,” he said, “as you go into battle, you ought to remember your name and race. No one in the Roman world has escaped your hands. For how did you give this name to all lands except by conquering? You must also remember the place where you now are and those against whom you Romans wage war. For we stand at the furthest part of the world. In crossing so great an expanse of lands, you have therefore seen nothing belonging to others. For what belongs to others when the whole world is in your possession? Whatever exists anywhere is yours by right; whatever all peoples inhabit is your possession. You were running well. Who has halted your triumphs as they ran throughout the world? Those triumphs which Hasdrubal the Carthaginian could not halt, nor Pyrrhus the Aeacid, nor Brennus pressing upon the approaches to the Capitol, nor the Persian hordes, nor the Egyptian phalanxes—rebellious Judaea has halted them, displaying an unskilled rashness in warfare, fitter for a brawl than a battle. Yet this is not what I fear. I consider it full of shame that you grow weary of conquering while those who are conquered so often have taken courage; that you are wearied by prosperity while they grow harder in adversity. Raise your spirits, then, men of Rome, and rise against the enemy hordes in confidence in your native valour. Do not let the numbers of the Jewish people disturb you, when they are not deterred by so many proofs of our valour, which are far stronger than numbers. For the Hebrews have neither knowledge of military affairs nor experience in fighting nor a gift for command, no practice of discipline, no patience to endure. They bring to battle only contempt for death; but no one has ever conquered an enemy by dying, only by killing. They know weapons only in war; we train with weapons in peace, so that in war we do not feel war’s uncertain chances. For the inexperienced, the outcome is doubtful; for veterans, triumph is customary. What else do we do every day but ensure that battles are never new to us? Each man trains at home as though in battle, so that in battle there is a kind of rehearsal of the contest. Indeed, no one would be mistaken in saying that our rehearsals are wars without blood, our wars rehearsals. We advance into war protected on every side: the head is covered by a helmet, the chest by a breastplate, and the whole body by a shield. The enemy can find nowhere to strike the Roman soldier, whom he sees enclosed in iron. Such arms are a burden to others, a covering for us, since practice makes them light. Thus our battle is against men unarmed and naked. Or do we fear being surrounded by their numbers? First, cavalry have freedom of movement in battle, making a game of war by retreating and pursuing; they ride round battle lines however great, and withdraw over whatever distances they please. Then, even in infantry combat, it is not so much the numbers of the many that decide the battle as the valour of the few. A multitude unused to discipline is its own hindrance: in prosperity, to victory; in adversity, to flight. But steadfast valour grows stronger in prosperity and does not collapse altogether in adversity. There is also this: our habit of victory is an incentive to fight. Even if they fight for their country and children, they ought not therefore to be readier than we are. For it is no less—indeed, I do not know whether it is not even more—to fight for ourselves than for our own people. We fight for ourselves when we fight for glory, so that we may not become less than we are. Who, then, could doubt that it is greater to fight for glory than for safety? But for us this war concerns the danger to our reputation, lest the right we have won be lost. We also risk appearing equal to the Jews, though we are conquerors of nations and rulers of the world: we set them up as opponents equal to ourselves if we engage them only with equal numbers. Our ancestors often routed great enemy forces with a small band. And what benefit do our daily exercises bring us, what our daily toil, if we come to battle with equal numbers? We have indeed reported their numbers to my father, because we were not permitted to do otherwise; but let him see that we have not feared the danger, but preserved our reverence for the arbiter of the war. We may taste the battle first, hold the enemy, seize victory while reinforcements are coming, lest those who arrive boast less that our common strength overcame the adversaries than that their valour protected us. With what face, then, shall we come before my father if we have feared to begin the battle? With what shame shall I, a degenerate son, meet the eyes of so great a man, who does not know what it is to see his soldier as anything but a victor? How shall I prove myself his son, when he is always triumphant but I am defeated even in my own judgement—which is worse—having yielded to a Jewish enemy? What will become of you when your commander is condemned, the man whom my father confidently entrusted to you? But I would rather you had to plead your case over your commander’s valour than over his cowardice. Let us therefore rush upon our adversaries, hasten, forestall the enemy. I shall run first into danger; follow, so that you may guard my father’s deposit and preserve what my father has entrusted to you. I ask for companions not in danger but in victory. Yet take care not to seem to have reserved for others the palm of triumph offered to you, and snatched it from yourselves. Certainly, if things turn out otherwise, I would rather my father recognised his son in my wounds, if he has not recognised him in his soldiers. But let us suppose that my father is offended by our beginning the battle. Which, then, is more bearable: to have seized victory too soon, or to have abandoned it? In seizing it too soon there is the haste of courage; in abandoning it, the fault of cowardice. Let my father condemn us as victors: I do not shrink from guilt of this kind. I would rather be guilty with the commonwealth triumphant than innocent with it injured. If only I might imitate the son of Manlius Torquatus, even in the danger alone, whom his father ordered to be struck with the axe because he had led the army against the enemy contrary to his father’s command! The young man stood with the enemy slain, clothed in triumphal glory, untroubled by death beneath the executioner, since he thought it the greatest happiness to die in victory. For what is more illustrious than to close one’s life with a triumph and not be kept for the uncertainty of events after a certain victory? O charge of victory, which the wise should seek! If only we too were accused of having conquered! Certainly, on that example, I alone shall be in danger; you will triumph. Yet my father has not forbidden us to fight, but commanded it by sending us into battle. Hence I think he will be angrier that we yielded to the Jews when we could conquer them than that we fought.”

[III.25.1] With these words he was the first to drive his horse against the enemy, and the others followed with a great shout, spreading across the whole plain, which made them seem more numerous. Trajan too arrived with three hundred cavalry, sent by Vespasian when Titus was already advancing. The Jews could not resist much longer, thrown into confusion by the men’s lances and the horses’ snorting. They therefore turned in different directions, many making for the city. Titus sprang forward, overwhelmed some as they fled with their backs turned and cut down others as they strayed. By forestalling their route he drove them all away from the walls and, meeting those who ran back, cut off their flight. Nevertheless, while some were struck down, others escaped and found refuge in the city.

[III.25.2] But there too the battle was fiercer. Those who had come from the neighbouring places at the beginning preferred peace, but the people who arrived later had forced them into support for the war against their will. Hence there was dissension and a grievous tumult within the city. Roused by the noise, Titus turned to his soldiers. “This, most faithful fellow soldiers,” he said, “is the moment I was seeking. The enemy stir up disturbances among themselves within the city: outside they are cut down, inside they fight with swords. Let us hasten while they are still divided, lest fear of danger bring them to reconciliation.”

[III.25.3] He therefore mounted the horse from which he had dismounted near the walls and, turning towards the lake, made for the city through the waves. He was the first to burst into the city, and the others followed him. At once all those within scattered in flight. Some were struck down, others boarded vessels and sank into the lake; many people were killed inside. Those from the countryside, however, offered themselves to the Romans, declaring that they had no part in the guilt. Titus, with merciful restraint, thought they should be spared, pressing only those responsible for the rebellion.

[III.25.4] He also sent a horseman to his father to announce the victory. Vespasian rejoiced at it, especially at his son’s triumph, for he had completed the greatest part of the whole war being waged against Judaea. He hastened there and ordered the city to be guarded more carefully so that no one could slip away, because all were liable to punishment. On another day, however, he ordered rafts to be made because of those who had taken to the boats. They were made without delay, since the neighbouring woods and the many workmen made it possible to hasten the task.

[III.26.1] For the lake itself, with a very broad expanse like a sea’s circuit, stretches a hundred and forty stades in length and spreads forty in breadth. Its rippling waters raise a breeze for it from itself, whence it is called Gennesar, a Greek word signifying, as it were, that it generates a breeze for itself. Its water is fresh and fit for drinking, receiving none of the thickness or turbidity of marshy moisture, since it is surrounded on every side by a sandy shore. It is more temperate than the chill of a river or spring, yet colder than the surface of a still marsh, precisely because the water does not lie flat like a pond but is stirred more often by blowing breezes across the lake’s wider spaces. Hence a draught of it is purer and softer for drinking. If anyone wishes to add care to its natural excellence and prepare it for drinking by hanging it out in the air on summer nights, as the inhabitants do, he would think it scarcely different from snow. Its kinds of fish too are superior in taste and appearance to those of another lake. The subject seems to require that we explain the source of the Jordan, as we promised elsewhere. For when men of an earlier age were uncertain whether the Jordan arose from the lake named Gennesar, Philip, tetrarch of the region of Trachonitis, refuted the false opinion and dispelled the error by throwing straw into Phiala, which the river threw up at Panium. It is therefore clear that Panium is not the Jordan’s source but a place where it flows. Its spring is not there, as though it began there in the manner of other rivers: it is brought there from Phiala by underground passages. There it wells up again like a spring and is revealed as it emerges. Phiala is in the land of Trachonitis, a hundred and twenty stades from the city of Caesarea. Its appearance gave Phiala its name, as though expressing the shape of a wheel, for it is so constantly full of water that the water neither overflows nor is perceived to be drawn away by any decrease. The water therefore flows below in a certain measure and wells up again at Panium, as the reappearance of the straw made plain. Thus the Jordan was shown to have risen again where men of an earlier time had thought it was born. Yet Panium did not have the same splendour from the beginning, only its natural beauty. Through Agrippa’s royal munificence a richer and more splendid adornment was added to the place; by it, we are told, the cave through which the Jordan rises was built up and beautified with admirable decoration. From there it begins to spread, no longer by a hidden course concealed in the earth’s hollows, but in a visible and open stream over the land. It cuts through Lake Semechonitis and its marshes. Then, directing its course, it proceeds a hundred and twenty stades without any mingling as far as the city named Julias. Afterwards it passes through the middle of the lake called Gennesar. From there, after wandering through many deserts, it is received by Lake Asphaltites and buried in it. Thus, after emerging victorious from two lakes, it remains caught in the third.

[III.26.2] The region of Gennesar stretches along the lake of the same name, from which it too took its name, with a marvellous natural grace and appearance of beauty. The fertility of the soil supplies spontaneous fruits; rich in groves, it raises itself of its own accord into every kind of fruit-bearing tree. The ingenuity of cultivation, imitating nature, has turned the gift of abundant fertility to whatever uses it wished, so that there is nothing there which nature has denied, nothing which cultivation has passed over. The air is suited to all fruits and never unfavourable to any, so temperate that it accommodates the diversity of everything that grows. There both what is nourished by cold and what is fostered by heat spread in abundance. There you may see summer growth mixed with winter growth, northern nuts together with dates which know no birth except in hotter places. Why speak of figs or olives, nourished by a milder stretch of sky? Yet they do not equal those mentioned before. For the former are the principal fruits of Palestine and, in a sense, native to it, and therefore more abundant; the latter are their near equals and, though separated by a long distance, nevertheless come next. You might call it a pleasing contest between nature and the seasons: nature, like a fruitful mother, creates everything; the temperateness of the seasons, like a good nurse, rears everything with gentle nurture. Thus not only are diverse fruits produced abundantly, but they are also preserved, so that some kinds do not fail for the greater part of the year, while all the rest last through the entire year to its end. For grapes and figs, which among cultivated fruits possess a certain royal grace, abound for ten months without any failure. The other fruits of the branches, whether the willing fields have produced them spontaneously or human industry has brought them into being, do not know how to abandon their service until new ones succeed them, following as it were the practice of attendants. To this fertility of nature and temperateness of the air is added the benefit of a spring, which irrigates the aforesaid region with a life-giving flow. Its name is Capharnaum. Some have thought, not without reason, that it is a vein of the river Nile, not only because its richness makes the fields fertile, but also because it produces a fish of such a kind that you would take it for the coracinus found in the lake at Alexandria through the Nile’s inflow. The district too, named after the lake, stretches thirty stades in length and twenty in breadth. Since we have spoken of the nature of the place, let us return to the conclusion of the battle.

[III.26.3] When the rafts had been prepared according to his command, Vespasian put a force of soldiers aboard to pursue those who had escaped destruction by fleeing in vessels. They could find no course to take. There was no place of safety on land, with the enemy surrounding everything; no possibility of flight on the water, since the lake was enclosed and surrounded on every side by Romans; no confidence even in resisting in their small light vessels. For what could a few do against so many as the rafts drew near? The rafts’ approach was indeed slower and the vessels’ sorties more effective, but the Romans suffered no wound: only the rattle of shields was heard as the missiles bounced off them. The Jews did not dare approach, and no one brought a boat nearer with impunity, since at close quarters it was easy to be struck by missiles or sunk by the rafts. If anyone tried to swim clear or rise to the surface, he was pierced by an arrow and gave up his wretched life in the waves. They could not resist much longer, as their numbers were reduced in different ways. Little by little, as more rafts converged, the Romans drove the greatest number of vessels towards the shores. Hemmed in there, they either leapt ashore and were killed there by the Romans, or were cut down by those pressing them from the rafts, or were crushed by the collision of rafts, or threw themselves into the lake when the enemy leapt into their boats. You could have seen the waters mingled with blood, the lake full of corpses. No one encountered was spared. The smell was grievous, the stench of the place utterly foul. Six thousand seven hundred Jews were killed in that battle, including, however, those killed earlier.

[III.26.4] Vespasian returned victorious to Taricheae. There he prepared to separate the people of the region from the townspeople, so that those who had not been responsible for the sedition might be spared. But many advised that allowing so great a multitude to survive, capable of renewing the fighting, was contrary to peace and harmful to the district. Where would they settle, driven from their homeland? On what food would they sustain themselves, deprived of everything, unless they lived by plunder? He changed his decision and, having inspired hope of being spared death, ordered them to leave by the gate facing Tiberias and make for that city. They readily believed what they desired. They began to leave, but the whole route had been occupied beforehand: the passing columns of Jews were hemmed in and led into the city’s stadium. Vespasian too entered and inspected the age and strength of all those whom he had ordered to be set before him. He selected six thousand of the stronger young men and sent them to Nero at the Isthmus. He ordered twelve hundred old and infirm men to be killed, and sold thirty thousand four hundred of the rest. All who were found to come from the territories of Agrippa’s kingdom he gave to the king, who likewise accepted payment and transferred them into the service of slavery. In addition, other people of the regions of Trachonitis and Gaulanitis, and the Hippeni and Gadarenes, paid just and deserved penalties for their crimes as instigators of war and disturbers of concord: they had abandoned their own lands and invaded those of others, taking up arms and violating the peace.
